title: Water is one of the most ordinary things in your life.
paragraphs: Water is one of the most ordinary things in your life.

You drink it.
You wash with it.
You pass by it without thinking twice.

But in Scripture…
water is never just water.

It is a boundary.
It is a dividing line.
It is the place where something ends… and something else begins.
And if you read carefully, you’ll notice a pattern:
God often does His deepest work in moments that involve water.

In the beginning, before anything was formed,
“the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters” (Genesis 1:2).

Before light.
Before land.
Before life as we know it.
There was water… and there was God preparing to create something new.
Water was there at the threshold of creation.
And then again… in Noah’s story.

The flood wasn’t just judgment.
It was a reset.

The old world, corrupted and broken, was washed away.
And when the waters receded, Noah didn’t just step onto dry ground…
He stepped into a new beginning.
Sometimes God allows the flood… because He’s preparing a fresh start.
Then comes Israel.
Trapped between Pharaoh’s army and the Red Sea.

No escape.
No strategy.
No way forward.
And yet, God didn’t build them a bridge.
He made them walk through the water.

Because freedom didn’t come by going around the obstacle…
it came by passing through it.

And when they reached the other side,
they were no longer slaves.
The same water that looked like a barrier… became the doorway to deliverance.

Naaman had power.
Status.
Authority.
But he also had leprosy.

And when God chose to heal him, He didn’t do it in a palace.
He didn’t do it through something impressive.
He told him to dip in the Jordan River.
Seven times.

It sounded too simple.
Too ordinary.
Almost offensive.

But when Naaman obeyed,
he came out of the water completely restored.
Don’t underestimate what God can do through simple obedience.
And then we arrive at the most personal expression of this symbol:
Baptism.
Romans 6:4 says we are “buried with Him through baptism into death… that we also should walk in newness of life.”
Read that again.

Buried.
Raised.
Newness of life.

Baptism is not just a religious act.
It is a declaration.
It is you saying:

“My old self is gone.”
“My past does not define me.”
“I am not who I used to be.”
When you go into the water, it represents death to your old life.

When you come out…
it represents resurrection.

God doesn’t just clean you up.
He makes you new.
And maybe that’s the part many people miss.

We try to “fix” ourselves.
Improve ourselves.
Manage our flaws.
But the Gospel is not about self-improvement.
It’s about transformation.
It’s about becoming someone entirely different because of what Christ has done.
Water carries that message all throughout Scripture:
You can begin again.

Not because you’re strong enough.
Not because you’re perfect.
But because God is merciful.
Because Jesus died… and rose again… so you could too.

Spiritually.
Internally.
Completely.
And here’s the question that lingers:

What part of your old life are you still holding onto…
that God is asking you to release?
Because new life requires surrender.

You cannot step into what God has for you…
while clinging to what He’s calling you out of.
Water is an invitation.

An invitation to let go.
An invitation to trust.
An invitation to be made new.
And maybe today, this isn’t just a message you read.
Maybe it’s a moment.
A moment where God is gently reminding you:

You are not stuck.
You are not disqualified.
You are not beyond redemption.
There is still new life available for you.
All throughout Scripture, water whispers the same truth:
“It’s not over.”

Engagement Question:
If you’re honest, what is one thing from your “old life” that you know God is asking you to leave behind today?
